cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Entertainment
cards.back: Roman entertainment served political purposes — panem et circenses (bread and circuses) kept the population content

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Entertainment
cards.back: Gladiatorial games (munera) originated as funeral rites and evolved into mass entertainment

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Entertainment
cards.back: The Colosseum (Flavian Amphitheatre) could hold 50,000-80,000 spectators and hosted gladiatorial combat and animal hunts

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Entertainment
cards.back: Gladiators were usually slaves, prisoners of war or condemned criminals — though some volunteered for fame and money

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Entertainment
cards.back: Different gladiator types: murmillo, retiarius, thraex, secutor — each had specific weapons and armour

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Entertainment
cards.back: The venatio (animal hunt) involved exotic animals from across the empire — elephants, lions, bears and tigers

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Entertainment
cards.back: Chariot racing at the Circus Maximus was the most popular entertainment — it could hold 250,000 spectators

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Entertainment
cards.back: Four racing factions (Red, White, Blue, Green) inspired fierce fan loyalty and sometimes riots

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Entertainment
cards.back: Theatre included comedy (Plautus, Terence) and satire — Roman audiences were rowdy and vocal

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Entertainment
cards.back: Emperors used games to display generosity, distract from political problems and demonstrate Roman power

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Entertainment
cards.back: The arena displayed Roman dominance over nature (animal hunts) and enemies (executions and re-enactments)

cards.front: Recall a key point about Roman Entertainment
cards.back: Public entertainment was free or cheap — it was a way for the elite to fulfil their political obligations
